questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Define the power of judicial review
questions.stem: In a clinician's note reviewing a patient's chart, the writer explains what it means for courts to review the constitutionality of laws.

answer.exemplar: Judicial review means that courts may examine whether a law, or an official act, conflicts with the constitution, and may refuse to give that law effect where the conflict is real. It does not mean that courts rewrite statutes, and it does not mean that courts have a general licence to substitute their judgment for the legislature's. It is a power to test law against a higher standard and, where the test fails, to withhold the ordinary enforcement that law would otherwise command.

questions.explanation: The power lets courts test law against the constitution and withhold enforcement, without letting courts redraw the statute. The tempting wrong idea is that review lets judges substitute their own policy.
questions.hint: Ask what the court withholds, not what it writes.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the text does not expressly grant judicial review
questions.stem: A clinician's note about a patient's records asks why the constitution does not expressly grant the power of judicial review.

answer.exemplar: The text does not describe the power because the framers expected it to follow from the document's structure: the constitution was declared to be the supreme law, so a conflicting law had to yield, and something had to decide the conflict. Early practice and argument supplied the mechanism, with the judiciary taking the role, and the political branches accepting it rather than stripping the courts of jurisdiction. The power rests on the constitution's supremacy rather than on a single clause.

questions.explanation: The power rests on the constitution's supremacy and on settled practice, not on an express clause. The tempting wrong idea is that the courts seized the power against the other branches' consent.
questions.hint: Think about what the supremacy of the text required.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Describe the limits observed in judicial review
questions.stem: A clinician's teaching note explains the limits courts observe when they examine a law for constitutionality.

answer.exemplar: Courts do not review laws for wisdom, policy, or economic convenience. They ask whether the law was made by a body with the authority the constitution gave it, whether it pursues a legitimate constitutional end, and whether the means are appropriate to that end. Where a law rests on a real granted power and a legitimate aim, a court may not substitute its own view of how the country should be governed for the judgment of the elected representatives who made the law.

questions.explanation: Review tests authority, aim, and fit, not policy wisdom. The tempting wrong idea is that courts may invalidate any law they consider unwise or unfair.
questions.hint: Separate questions of power from questions of policy.

questions.learningObjective: Assess whether judicial review is the final word
questions.stem: A clinician's note about a patient's treatment plan asks whether judicial review means courts have the last word on any dispute.

answer.exemplar: Judicial review is not a claim to the last word on every dispute. options.text: The longer terms allow that chamber to choose its own members in the interim
options.misconception: invents interim elections for a chamber

options.text: The two term lengths are two parts of one design balancing stability and responsiveness
The longer terms make that chamber unnecessary for routine lawmaking
options.misconception: claims a term rule makes a chamber redundant

questions.explanation: The two term lengths together deliver quick responsiveness and institutional continuity within a single coordinated design. The tempting wrong idea is that the longer terms create a separate veto power.
questions.hint: Ask what the two lengths accomplish together.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why impeachment does not bar other proceedings
questions.stem: A clinician's note about a patient's chart asks why a person convicted by the senate may still face a separate legal proceeding. Which reason fits?

options.text: Because impeachment is a political remedy and criminal charges are a separate matter
options.misconception: reverses the two kinds of proceeding

options.text: Because the senate's conviction is only a recommendation to the ordinary courts
options.misconception: reduces impeachment to a mere recommendation

options.text: Because criminal charges may only be brought in the year after the impeachment trial
options.misconception: invents a timing rule for criminal prosecutions

options.text: Because the senate's verdict does not prevent an ordinary criminal case being brought

questions.explanation: The impeachment verdict answers a political question about fitness for office and does not foreclose an ordinary criminal prosecution on the same conduct. The tempting wrong idea is that the senate's verdict is only a suggestion to the courts.
questions.hint: Ask what the verdict settles and what it leaves open.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the requirement for consent to treaties
questions.stem: A clinician's note about a patient's records asks about the consent requirement for treaties, which appear alongside appointments. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: The executive may make treaties, but two thirds of the senate must consent to them
The executive may make treaties, and a simple majority of the senate must consent
options.misconception: lowers the treaty consent threshold to a simple majority

options.text: The senate may make treaties once it has consent from the house
options.misconception: reverses which branch negotiates and which consents

options.text: Treaties require the consent of every state legislature before the senate may act
options.misconception: invents a state role in the treaty consent power

questions.explanation: The executive negotiates treaties but two thirds of the senate must consent, which puts a durable check on the most lasting external commitments. The tempting wrong idea is that a simple majority of the senate is enough.
questions.hint: Ask what fraction of the senate must agree.
